name: Luxury editorial
philosophy: Communicate material, authorship and care through specific imagery and deliberate pacing. Luxury is supported by useful product information and service, not by hiding price or navigation.
influences: Editorial art direction, exhibition catalogs and product photography inform this contemporary recipe. Avoid presenting a serif face or beige palette as historical proof of luxury.
characteristics: A serif or expressive display voice balanced by readable utility text
Selective contrast between generous narrative space and compact purchasing details
typography: Test a display serif at its intended optical size; fine hairlines can fail at small sizes. Keep product details and booking controls sturdy. Begin with Georgia and a system sans when licensed assets are unavailable; select a final font through real-language specimens.
color: Draw the palette from materials and photography. Dark ink on a light ground is one option, not a mandate. Gold is a material cue only when relevant; pale gold body text usually weakens legibility.
spacing: Separate narrative chapters generously, but keep price, variants, availability and purchase action close. A 24px control group gap should not become a 120px mobile dead zone.
composition: Use image-led chapters with varying scale and restrained text columns. Product detail pages need a stable action area and direct access to sizing, delivery and returns.
imagery: Art-direct a consistent light direction, crop family and material detail. Missing photographs are a production dependency, not permission to invent a product rendering or testimonials.
iconography: Few simple controls, paired with words where ambiguity affects purchase. Decorative crests and pseudo-heritage seals require a real brand reason.
components: Product selectors expose selected and unavailable states. Show total price and practical service details. Editorial pull quotes need attribution, not fictional endorsements.
interaction: Image zoom must have a keyboard-accessible alternative. Swatches update the relevant image and textual color name. Avoid hover-only discovery.
motion: A gentle crossfade may connect product views. Preserve scroll control; cinematic chapters need a static reduced-motion version and visible navigation.
mobile: Prioritize product, price, options and purchase action before long brand narrative. Keep image focal points visible. A sticky purchase bar must not cover content or focus.
accessibility: Check text over every image crop, not just the desktop hero. Provide meaningful product descriptions and avoid disabling zoom.
mistakes: Thin pale text treated as sophistication
Stock scenes unrelated to the offer
Unreachable purchase controls below an oversized introduction
amateurish: A generic serif, large whitespace and gold accents without material specificity or complete buying information.
exceptional: The image, copy, detail hierarchy and service flow convey the same product quality. Deliberate quietness survives mobile and error states.
implementation: Use figure/figcaption for material stories, aspect-ratio for stable images and object-position per crop. Separate display and control tokens. Do not bind layout to a fixed viewport height.
libraries: Native responsive images and CSS are enough for most pages. Adopt a dialog primitive only when zoom or a size guide requires it.
evaluation: Is the product's material or provenance demonstrated?
Can a mobile visitor find price, availability and service terms?
Do all controls remain robust when the display type is removed?
evidence: Original design recipe; source-linked engineering constraints. Not a validated causal model of visual quality.
